title: He just collapsed: a witnessed in-hospital collapse in a 64-year-old man on a regional medical ward (Code Blue)
desc: This station starts with a Code Blue on a medical ward in a regional hospital. The candidate is the first to arrive. Collin Barker, 64, was admitted last night with an NSTEMI and is waiting for transfer for coronary angiography. He collapsed while a third-year medical student was taking his history. In Part 1 the candidate runs basic life support (DRSABCD) on a manikin, with the examiner giving findings and asking questions: airway adjuncts and sizing a Guedel, CPR, and a safe shock when the AED advises one. Once the Code Blue team takes over, the candidate takes a focused collateral history from the student, the nurse and the chart, including his resuscitation status. In Part 2 the candidate interprets the defibrillator rhythm strip (ventricular fibrillation), a venous blood gas taken during CPR and his troponin and electrolyte results. They then hand over in ISBAR format, name the most likely cause and the reversible causes, outline advanced life support with drug timing and post-ROSC disposition, and contrast shockable with non-shockable rhythms.
focus: Running DRSABCD for a witnessed in-hospital collapse, recognising VF and applying the ANZCOR adult ALS algorithm, including the reversible causes
stem:
You are a final-year medical student on placement on a general medical ward at a regional hospital. A Code Blue is called and you are the first to arrive at the bedside. The patient is Collin Barker, a 64-year-old man. A terrified third-year medical student, Sam, says: “I was taking a history from this patient, Collin, then he suddenly collapsed so I called a Code Blue. I don’t know what to do!”

The Code Blue team is on its way. A resuscitation manikin is in the bed in place of Collin. Say aloud what you are checking and doing, and the examiner will tell you what you find.
tasks: Assess and begin resuscitating Collin, telling the examiner what you are examining and doing. Then take a focused history from Sam, the ward nurse and the chart (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you the defibrillator rhythm strip, a venous blood gas taken during CPR and Collin's blood results. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and answer a focused question (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You play Sam, a third-year medical student on your first medical placement. You were taking a history from Collin Barker when he collapsed. You are frightened and shaky and you talk too fast. You calm down once the candidate gives you a clear job (for example, bringing the defibrillator, noting the time or taking a turn at compressions). The examiner gives the findings on the manikin and speaks for the ward nurse, RN Kate Nguyen, and the Code Blue team.

Opening line: “I was taking a history from this patient, Collin, then he suddenly collapsed so I called a Code Blue. I don’t know what to do!”

How the scene runs (examiner)

  1. First minutes: the candidate works through DRSABCD and the examiner gives the findings below. If the candidate asks for the defibrillator and the resuscitation trolley, Kate (or Sam, if sent) brings them about a minute later. If nobody asks, Kate brings them at about 2 minutes so the scenario can continue, but the candidate does not earn item 15.
  2. Defibrillator: it is used in AED (automatic) mode. Once the pads are on, the AED analyses and says “Shock advised. Stand clear.” When the candidate has made sure everyone is clear and the shock is given, it says “Shock delivered. Start CPR.” Collin does not respond.
  3. Team arrives (about 4 to 5 minutes in): the medical registrar takes over as team leader. The ICU nurse takes the airway and a ward nurse takes over compressions. The registrar says: “Thanks. Can you find out everything you can about Collin from the student, the nurse and the chart?” The rest of Part 1 is the collateral history.
  4. If the candidate does not start compressions: after the breathing check, the examiner says once: “What do you do now?” Give no further hints.

What Sam knows (give only when asked)

  • Just before the collapse: Collin had been chatting normally. At about 10:38 he said his chest was going tight again, “the same as last night”, about 6 out of 10, in the middle of his chest. He went pale and sweaty and said, “I feel funny, my heart’s racing.”
  • The collapse: at about 10:41 he slumped sideways in the bed. His eyes rolled up, and his arms and legs jerked for a few seconds. Then he made a few slow, noisy, snoring gasps and went still. You saw it happen.
  • Calling for help: you pressed the emergency buzzer and the Code Blue was called at 10:42. You did not start CPR because you “froze”.
  • Ruling out other causes: he was not eating or drinking, so he could not have choked. He was sitting in bed and did not hit his head. He did not bite his tongue (as far as you saw) and did not wet himself. He has never had a seizure.
  • Why he is in hospital: he came in through ED last night with 2 hours of tight central chest pain going into his left arm, with sweating. He told you the doctors said it was “a heart attack” and that he is waiting for a bed at the city hospital “to have the tubes in my heart looked at”.
  • Past history: type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure and high cholesterol. He has never had heart problems before.
  • Social: a retired farmer. He smokes 20 cigarettes a day and drinks a few beers on weekends. He lives with his wife, Margaret, about 30 minutes out of town.
  • Allergies: he told you he has none.

What RN Kate Nguyen and the chart give (when the candidate asks the nurse or looks in the chart)

  • Resuscitation plan: completed on admission last night after discussion with Collin and Margaret: for full resuscitation.
  • Medication chart: aspirin 100 mg daily (300 mg loading dose in ED), ticagrelor 90 mg twice daily (180 mg loading dose in ED), enoxaparin 90 mg SC twice daily (last dose 08:00), metoprolol 25 mg twice daily, atorvastatin 80 mg nightly, GTN spray when needed. His usual perindopril with indapamide and his metformin are also charted. He has had no GTN since last night.
  • Observations at 09:30: RR 16, SpO2 96% on room air, BP 132/80, HR 78 and regular, temperature 36.7 °C, alert, pain 0. No cardiac monitoring was in place.
  • Admission ECG: sinus rhythm at 84/min with 1 to 2 mm ST depression in V4 to V6, I and aVL, and no ST elevation. The 06:00 ECG is unchanged.
  • Bloods: “The morning bloods came back at about 10:15. His troponin has gone up a lot. The lab rang about his magnesium being low, and his potassium is low too. The resident was about to chart replacement but hadn’t yet.” (The numbers are handed over in Part 2.)
  • Next of kin: his wife, Margaret, at home. Her number is on the front of the chart.

Feelings, ideas, concerns and expectations (Sam)

  • You are terrified and feel guilty: “Did I do something? I was just asking him questions.”
  • You expect the candidate to tell you what to do.

Question to raise once the team has arrived: “Is he going to be OK?” Accept a brief, honest answer.

Exam findings (examiner: give only when the candidate says what they are checking or doing)

  • On arrival: Collin is half sitting up in bed, slumped to the left, grey, with his eyes half open. He has a 20 G IV cannula in his left forearm and no monitoring attached.
  • Danger: no hazards. The floor is dry, the bed is electric and working, no oxygen is running and there are no sharps. If the candidate asks, the bed can be laid flat with the backrest down, and a CPR board is on the trolley.
  • Response: no response to voice (“Collin, can you hear me? Open your eyes. Squeeze my hand”), to a firm shoulder squeeze, or to trapezius or sternal pressure.
  • Airway: no visible foreign body. There is a gurgling sound with secretions at the back of the mouth. Examiner prompt: “The airway isn’t patent. What do you insert?” If asked, Yankauer suction clears the secretions. Once a Guedel is in place, the airway is patent. Then ask: “How do you size a Guedel?”
  • Breathing: after up to 10 seconds of looking, listening and feeling, Collin is not breathing normally: there is one slow gasp only. If a carotid pulse is felt at the same time: no pulse.
  • During CPR: the chest rises with each bag-valve-mask breath. If the candidate has not named the device, ask: “What device are you using to give the breaths?”
  • IV access: the 20 G cannula in the left forearm flushes easily.
  • After the shock: no change. Collin remains unresponsive, without normal breathing.

check.x: Professionalism
Introduces self and role to Sam, stays calm and takes charge, and gives Sam a clear task (e.g. bring the defibrillator and resuscitation trolley, note the time, take a turn at compressions).

Communicates clearly with closed loops: says each step aloud and checks instructions are heard (e.g. "Hands off, stand clear"). Gives a brief handover to the team leader when the Code Blue team arrives and accepts a role.
History
Establishes from Sam what happened before and during the collapse:

kids.x: Chest tightness came back a few minutes before the collapse ("the same as last night"), with pallor, sweating and "my heart's racing".
Witnessed collapse in bed at about 10:41, with the Code Blue called at 10:42; not eating (no choking) and no head strike.
Clarifies the jerking: a few seconds of jerks, then slow noisy gasps; no tongue biting and no previous seizures.

check.x: Establishes why Collin is in hospital: chest pain last night, diagnosed as an NSTEMI, waiting for transfer for coronary angiography.
Confirms his resuscitation status from the nurse or the chart: the admission resuscitation plan says for full resuscitation.
check.d: Award only once CPR has started; checking must not delay resuscitation.

check.x: Takes the medication and allergy history:

kids.x: Antithrombotics: aspirin, ticagrelor and therapeutic enoxaparin (last dose 08:00).
Other medicines: metoprolol, atorvastatin, perindopril with indapamide, and metformin. No allergies.

check.x: Takes the past history and risk factors: type 2 diabetes, hypertension, high cholesterol, smokes 20 a day; no previous heart disease.

Asks about recent observations and results: observations normal at 09:30; ST depression in V4 to V6, I and aVL on the admission ECG; morning bloods back, with a rising troponin and low magnesium and potassium not yet replaced.
Identifies the next of kin (his wife, Margaret, at home) so that she can be contacted.
Examination
Danger: checks for electrical, fluid and sharps hazards [none], and lays the bed flat on a firm surface (CPR board).
Response: talk and touch ("Collin, can you hear me? Open your eyes. Squeeze my hand") with a shoulder squeeze [no response].
check.d: Award for talk and touch with a shoulder squeeze; a trapezius or sternal stimulus is acceptable but not required.

check.x: Send for help: recognises that the Code Blue has already been called and the team is coming, and asks for the defibrillator and resuscitation trolley.
Airway:

kids.x: Opens the airway with head tilt and chin lift (or jaw thrust), looks for foreign material and listens [gurgling], and suctions the secretions.
Inserts an oropharyngeal (Guedel) airway when prompted; a nasopharyngeal airway is an acceptable alternative or addition.
Sizes the Guedel from the angle of the mandible to the centre of the incisors.
kids.d: Also accept the angle of the jaw to the corner of the mouth.

check.x: Breathing: looks, listens and feels for no more than 10 seconds, recognises the occasional gasp as abnormal breathing, and starts compressions straight away without delaying for a pulse check.
check.d: Do not award if CPR is delayed by a prolonged pulse check or by treating the gasps as breathing.

check.x: CPR:

kids.x: Compressions on the lower half of the sternum at 100 to 120 a minute, to one third of the chest depth, with full recoil and minimal interruptions.
30 compressions to 2 breaths using a bag-valve-mask with oxygen at 15 L/min and head tilt or jaw thrust (names the device).
kids.d: Award if the device is named only after the examiner asks.

kids.x: Rotates the person doing compressions every 2 minutes to avoid fatigue.

check.x: Defibrillation:

kids.x: Applies the pads as soon as the defibrillator arrives, while compressions continue, in the anterolateral position (below the right clavicle, and the left mid-axillary line at V6).
Pauses compressions only for the analysis. On "shock advised", makes sure everyone is clear and the oxygen is moved away, then shocks.
Restarts compressions immediately after the shock for 2 minutes, with no pulse or rhythm check.

check.x: Checks for IV access (the cannula in situ flushes) or asks for intraosseous access, ready for drugs.
Interpretation

Interprets the rhythm strip as ventricular fibrillation: chaotic, irregular deflections of varying amplitude with no identifiable P waves, QRS complexes or T waves, and no organised ventricular rate (fibrillatory activity at roughly 300 a minute). Notes that it persisted after the first shock and states that VF is a shockable rhythm.
check.d: Award for chaotic irregular deflections with no identifiable QRS complexes, identified as VF and shockable; a rate is not required.

check.x: Interprets the venous gas as a mixed respiratory and lactic acidosis expected in cardiac arrest, and notes that potassium 3.2 is low; glucose is not low and haemoglobin is normal.
check.d: Credit if given in the ISBAR or in the diagnosis answer.

check.x: Interprets the bloods: troponin rising from 46 to 412 to 2850 ng/L indicates an evolving NSTEMI; potassium 3.3 and magnesium 0.62 are low.
check.d: Credit indapamide as the likely cause of the low potassium and magnesium, but it is not required. Credit if given in the ISBAR or in the diagnosis answer.

check.x: Gives VF cardiac arrest from acute myocardial ischaemia (coronary thrombosis) as the most likely diagnosis, with hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia contributing, and justifies it from the history and results.

Names the reversible causes (4 Hs and 4 Ts): hypoxia; hypovolaemia; hypothermia or hyperthermia; hypokalaemia, hyperkalaemia and other metabolic causes; tension pneumothorax; tamponade; toxins; thrombosis (coronary or pulmonary).
Management
Continues ALS in 2-minute cycles: a single shock for VF, compressions straight after each shock and while the defibrillator charges, and a rhythm check every 2 minutes with minimal pauses.
Gives adrenaline 1 mg IV after the second shock (now due), then every second cycle (about every 4 minutes).
Gives amiodarone 300 mg IV after the third shock if VF persists.

Plans the airway and ventilation: an advanced airway (supraglottic airway or endotracheal tube) placed by a skilled operator without stopping compressions, then continuous compressions with about 10 breaths a minute, and waveform capnography.

Treats Collin's reversible causes: replaces potassium and magnesium with the team leader (ANZCOR: potassium chloride 5 mmol IV bolus for refractory VF with hypokalaemia; magnesium sulfate 5 mmol IV for hypomagnesaemia), and treats the acidosis with effective CPR and ventilation.
check.d: Award for replacing both potassium and magnesium without the exact doses.

check.x: Names the non-shockable rhythms (asystole and PEA) and states that for them adrenaline 1 mg is given as soon as access is available, then every second cycle, with no shocks.
Plans post-ROSC care and disposition:

kids.x: Disposition: ICU, and an urgent interventional cardiology discussion about emergency coronary angiography with retrieval to a PCI-capable centre.
Names at least two post-ROSC targets: 12-lead ECG, SpO2 92 to 98%, normal CO2, avoiding hypotension, checking glucose, preventing fever.

check.x: Safety netting
Makes sure his wife, Margaret, is contacted early by a senior clinician, and that the resuscitation is documented (times, rhythms, shocks and drugs).
check.d: Credit from the management answer or from the reply to Sam.

check.x: Supports Sam: tells Sam that calling the Code Blue promptly was right and that the collapse was not Sam's fault, and arranges a team debrief and follow-up support.
check.d: Credit from the response to Sam in Part 1 or Part 2.

part2.lead: It is now 10:47, one minute into the cycle after the second shock. Collin is still in cardiac arrest and the team is continuing CPR. The registrar has switched the defibrillator to manual mode. Here is the printed rhythm strip from the defibrillator, a venous blood gas taken during CPR, and Collin's blood results from admission and this morning.
part2.patient:
• Only if the candidate has not already reassured you in Part 1 (item 37 not yet earned): as the candidate finishes the management answer, Sam asks quietly: “Did I do something wrong? Should I have noticed sooner?” Settle if the candidate reassures you kindly and mentions a debrief.
  • If not already answered, ask: “Is he going to be OK?”

handover.label: Defibrillator rhythm strip (10:44 and 10:46)
handover.result:
Defibrillator printout, pads lead, 25 mm/s, 10 mm/mV. AED mode for the first analysis; manual mode from the second rhythm check.

  • First analysis, 10:44 (AED mode): fast, chaotic, irregular deflections that vary in amplitude and shape from moment to moment, at roughly 300 a minute. There are no identifiable P waves, QRS complexes or T waves and no organised rhythm, so no rate or intervals can be measured. Device message: shock advised. First shock (200 J biphasic) delivered at 10:44.
  • Second rhythm check, 10:46, after 2 minutes of CPR: manual mode, rhythm check by the team leader: VF, the same chaotic pattern with slightly lower amplitude; second shock (200 J biphasic) delivered at 10:46. CPR is continuing.
  • Comparison: the 06:00 12-lead ECG showed sinus rhythm at 80/min with 1 to 2 mm ST depression in V4 to V6, I and aVL.
handover.model:
• Read: chaotic, irregular deflections of varying amplitude, with no P waves, QRS complexes or T waves and no organised ventricular rate (fibrillatory activity at roughly 300 a minute; VF runs at roughly 150 to 500 a minute). This is coarse ventricular fibrillation, and it persisted after the first shock.
  • For Collin: VF is a shockable rhythm, as is pulseless VT; asystole and PEA are not. Before the collapse he had ischaemic chest pain and his ECG showed lateral ST depression, so VF from acute ischaemia fits.
  • What it changes: he stays on the shockable arm of the algorithm. Two shocks have been given, so adrenaline 1 mg IV is due now, during this cycle. If VF persists at the rhythm check at 10:48, give the third shock and then amiodarone 300 mg.

handover.label: Venous blood gas (during CPR, 10:45)
handover.result: Venous sample taken by femoral stab during CPR at 10:45 and run on the ward blood gas analyser (result 10:46).
handover.model:
• Read: pH 7.07 with a high pCO2 of 64 and a low HCO3 of 18, base excess −11 and lactate 8.4. This is a mixed respiratory and lactic metabolic acidosis. Potassium is low at 3.2. Sodium and ionised calcium are normal, glucose is high at 11.2 and haemoglobin is normal at 136.
  • For Collin: the acidosis is what is expected during an arrest (low blood flow and inadequate ventilation). It is treated with high-quality CPR and ventilation, not routine bicarbonate. The low potassium is a reversible contributor to VF. Hypoglycaemia is excluded. The normal haemoglobin argues against major bleeding on his antithrombotics.
  • What it changes: replace potassium (and magnesium) with the team leader, and repeat the gas.

handover.label: Blood results (admission, overnight and this morning)
handover.result: Morning sample collected at 06:00 and reported at 10:15. Low magnesium phoned to the ward RN at 10:15.
handover.model:
• Read: high-sensitivity troponin I rose from 46 to 412 to 2850 ng/L. Potassium has drifted down from 3.6 to 3.3 and magnesium is 0.62 (both low). Sodium, creatinine, eGFR, haemoglobin and platelets are normal.
  • For Collin: the steep troponin rise confirms an evolving myocardial infarction (NSTEMI), so ongoing coronary thrombosis is the most likely trigger of the VF. Low potassium and magnesium, probably from indapamide, make the myocardium more prone to VF and are reversible. Normal renal function makes hyperkalaemia from renal failure unlikely, and his haemoglobin and platelets argue against bleeding.
  • What it changes: replace potassium and magnesium. After ROSC he needs urgent cardiology input about emergency coronary angiography, with retrieval to a PCI-capable centre.

ask: The medical registrar leading the Code Blue has asked for a summary. Please give an ISBAR handover of Collin Barker, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Collin now, here on the ward.
Which cardiac arrest rhythms are shockable and which are non-shockable, and how would your management differ if Collin's rhythm became non-shockable?
expect:
• Identify: medical student; Collin Barker, 64, medical ward.
  • Situation: witnessed in-hospital cardiac arrest at 10:41; CPR started, 2 shocks given, still in VF.
  • Background: admitted last night with an NSTEMI, waiting for angiography; chest pain came back just before the collapse; diabetes, hypertension, smoker; on aspirin, ticagrelor, enoxaparin and indapamide; for full resuscitation.
  • Assessment: strip shows VF that persisted after the first shock. VBG shows a mixed acidosis expected in arrest, with K 3.2; glucose not low, Hb normal. Troponin 46 to 412 to 2850, Mg 0.62; K and Mg low, probably from indapamide; renal function normal. Ischaemic VF, with low K and Mg contributing.
  • Recommendation: adrenaline now; amiodarone after the third shock; replace K and Mg; after ROSC, ICU and urgent cardiology for angiography.

Most likely: VF cardiac arrest from acute myocardial ischaemia (evolving NSTEMI). For: ischaemic chest pain and palpitations just before a witnessed collapse, rising troponin, lateral ST depression, VF on the strip. Low K and Mg (indapamide) are contributing.

Reversible causes (4 Hs, 4 Ts) in Collin:

  • Hypoxia: unlikely; he was talking normally just before.
  • Hypovolaemia or bleeding: possible on antithrombotics, but Hb 136.
  • Hypothermia or hyperthermia: unlikely on a ward.
  • Hypokalaemia and metabolic: yes, K and Mg are low; glucose is not low.
  • Tension pneumothorax: no trauma or central line.
  • Tamponade: post-infarct rupture or bleeding is possible, but it usually causes PEA.
  • Toxins: none apparent.
  • Thrombosis: coronary (most likely); pulmonary is less likely because he is on therapeutic enoxaparin.

Credit naming the brief jerks as hypoxic jerking, not a seizure.

1. ALS: 2-minute cycles; single shocks for VF; compressions during charging and straight after each shock; minimal pauses.
  2. Drugs: adrenaline 1 mg IV now (after the second shock), then every second cycle; amiodarone 300 mg IV after the third shock.
  3. Airway: advanced airway by a skilled operator, then continuous compressions at about 10 breaths a minute; waveform capnography.
  4. Reversible causes: replace K and Mg (doses not required).
  5. After ROSC: ICU; urgent interventional cardiology discussion about emergency angiography; retrieval to a PCI centre. At least two targets: 12-lead ECG, SpO2 92 to 98%, normal CO2, avoid hypotension, check glucose, prevent fever.
  6. People: a senior calls his wife, Margaret; document; debrief and support Sam.

• Shockable: VF and pulseless VT.
  • Non-shockable: asystole and pulseless electrical activity (PEA).
  • Shockable arm: shock, then 2 minutes of CPR; adrenaline 1 mg after the second shock and then every second cycle; amiodarone 300 mg after the third shock.
  • Non-shockable arm: no shocks; adrenaline 1 mg IV as soon as access is available, then every second cycle (about every 4 minutes); 2-minute cycles of CPR; actively look for and treat reversible causes (in PEA after an MI, think of tamponade and bleeding).
  • Recheck the rhythm every 2 minutes and change arms if it changes.

ddx.dx: Ventricular fibrillation cardiac arrest from acute myocardial ischaemia (evolving NSTEMI)
ddx.for: Ischaemic chest pain and palpitations just before a witnessed collapse, a troponin rising from 46 to 2850 ng/L, lateral ST depression and VF on the strip.
He said his heart was racing before the collapse, and the AED advised a shock.
ddx.against: The strip shows chaotic deflections of varying amplitude with no organised QRS complexes.

ddx.dx: Arrhythmic arrest precipitated by hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia
ddx.for: Potassium 3.3 then 3.2 and magnesium 0.62 on indapamide, not yet replaced.
ddx.against: The derangement is mild, and acute ischaemia with recurrent chest pain is the more likely main trigger; it is a contributor.

ddx.for: Sam saw his arms and legs jerk for a few seconds as he collapsed.
ddx.against: He was pulseless and gasping, and the brief jerks followed chest pain and collapse, which fits hypoxic jerking from cardiac arrest.

ddx.for: A sudden collapse in a hospital inpatient.
ddx.against: He is on therapeutic enoxaparin, his chest pain was ischaemic rather than pleuritic, and the rhythm is VF rather than PEA.

ddx.dx: Cardiac tamponade (post-infarct free wall rupture or bleeding on anticoagulation)
ddx.for: An acute myocardial infarction treated with dual antiplatelets and therapeutic enoxaparin.
ddx.against: Rupture usually occurs days after infarction and presents with PEA, not VF, and his haemoglobin is normal.

guide:
Set-up: use a resuscitation manikin in a bed, a bag-valve-mask, Guedel airways, a Yankauer and a training defibrillator or AED if available. The person playing the patient plays Sam, the third-year student. The examiner gives the manikin findings and speaks for RN Kate Nguyen and the Code Blue team.

Part 1:

  • Time in the scenario is compressed. The defibrillator arrives about a minute after it is asked for, and the AED makes the shock decision, so the candidate does not have to interpret the rhythm in Part 1. The formal reading of the strip is marked in Part 2 (item 22).
  • Give the source's prompts exactly as written:
    • “The airway isn't patent. What do you insert?”
    • “How do you size a Guedel?”
    • “What device are you using to give the breaths?” (only if the candidate has not named it).
  • After the breathing check, give the occasional gasp. A safe candidate treats it as abnormal breathing and starts compressions at once. If a carotid pulse is felt at the same time for no more than 10 seconds, give “no pulse”; do not penalise this unless it delays compressions.
  • The candidate may say what they are doing while giving short bursts of compressions on the manikin. They do not need to do 2 minutes of compressions for real.
  • Bring the team in about 4 to 5 minutes into the station, after the first shock, so there is time for the collateral history.
  • Item 7 (resuscitation status) is credited only once CPR is under way. A candidate who stops to look for the plan before starting CPR does not earn item 17.

Part 2:

  • Hand over all three results together and ask the four questions in order.
  • Score items 22 to 24 from the ISBAR or the diagnosis answer, and items 25 to 26 from the diagnosis question.
  • Score items 28 to 32 and 34 from the management answer. Item 34 is critical on the disposition (ICU and urgent cardiology for angiography and retrieval) only.
  • Score item 33 from the fourth question; also credit the shockable-rhythm part of item 22 there.
  • Score item 36 from the management answer or the reply to Sam.
  • Score item 37 from the candidate's response to Sam in Part 1 or Part 2. Sam's Part 2 interjection about blame is used only if item 37 has not yet been earned.

A high-performing candidate takes charge calmly and gives Sam a job. They work through DRSABCD without hesitating, recognise the gasping as cardiac arrest and start good-quality compressions, and get the pads on and shock safely with minimal pauses. Once the team arrives, they find the recurrent chest pain, the NSTEMI, the antithrombotics, the indapamide and the low potassium and magnesium, and confirm his resuscitation status. In Part 2 they read the strip as VF, link the troponin and electrolytes to the cause, and give the drug timings correctly. They work through the 4 Hs and 4 Ts with reference to Collin and plan post-ROSC angiography.

A borderline candidate takes too long over the airway or a pulse check, treats the gasps as breathing, or is reassured that the jerks were “just a seizure”. They may stop compressions to check a pulse after the shock, give adrenaline before the second shock on the shockable arm, or forget amiodarone and the reversible causes.
explain:
The scenario: a witnessed in-hospital cardiac arrest

Collin was admitted with an NSTEMI and was waiting for coronary angiography. Minutes before he collapsed, his ischaemic chest pain came back with palpitations. He then lost consciousness, had brief jerks and made slow gasps. That is the typical sequence of a ventricular arrhythmia causing cardiac arrest. The brief jerks are myoclonic jerking from cerebral hypoperfusion. Slow, noisy gasps (agonal breathing) are not normal breathing. Both are common in the first minute of a cardiac arrest, and mistaking them for a seizure or for breathing delays CPR. Patients with an NSTEMI awaiting angiography should have continuous cardiac monitoring; an unmonitored arrest delays recognition and defibrillation.

Basic life support: DRSABCD (ANZCOR)

  • Danger: electrical, fluid, sharps and chemical hazards.
  • Response: talk and touch (“Can you hear me? Open your eyes. Squeeze my hand”), with a trapezius or sternal stimulus if there is no response.
  • Send for help: here the Code Blue has already been called. Ask for the defibrillator and resuscitation trolley, and give the frightened junior a clear task.
  • Airway: head tilt and chin lift (or jaw thrust). Look for foreign material and suction secretions. If the airway is still not patent, insert an oropharyngeal (Guedel) airway, sized from the angle of the mandible to the centre of the incisors; a nasopharyngeal airway is an alternative or addition.
  • Breathing: look, listen and feel for no more than 10 seconds. If the person is unresponsive and not breathing normally, start CPR. A pulse check is unreliable and must not delay compressions.
  • CPR: compressions on the lower half of the sternum, to one third of the chest depth, at 100 to 120 a minute, with full recoil. Give 30 compressions to 2 breaths by bag-valve-mask with oxygen. Rotate the person doing compressions every 2 minutes.
  • Defibrillation: attach the pads as soon as the defibrillator arrives, without stopping compressions. Pause only for the analysis. Make sure everyone is clear before the shock, then restart compressions immediately for 2 minutes with no pulse check.

Collateral history in a Code Blue

Once the team has taken over, the most useful information comes from the person who saw the collapse, the nurse and the chart:

  • what happened just before the collapse (here, recurrent ischaemic pain);
  • whether it was witnessed, and the time of collapse;
  • the reason for admission;
  • the resuscitation plan or goals of care;
  • medicines (antithrombotics, diuretics, QT-prolonging drugs);
  • recent results;
  • the next of kin.

Interpreting the rhythm

Read any ECG systematically: details, rate, rhythm, axis, P waves, PR (120 to 200 ms), QRS (under 120 ms), ST segments, T waves and QTc. In VF the strip shows chaotic, irregular deflections of varying amplitude at roughly 150 to 500 a minute, with no identifiable P waves, QRS complexes or T waves. Pulseless VT, by contrast, is a broad-complex tachycardia with organised QRS complexes: regular if monomorphic, and varying in a twisting pattern in polymorphic VT or torsades (think magnesium).

  • Shockable rhythms: VF and pulseless VT.
  • Non-shockable rhythms: asystole and pulseless electrical activity.

Advanced life support (ANZCOR adult ALS algorithm)

  • Run CPR in 2-minute cycles, checking the rhythm at the end of each cycle with minimal pauses, and charge the defibrillator during compressions (in manual mode).
  • Shockable rhythm:
    • Give single shocks, each followed straight away by 2 minutes of CPR.
    • Give adrenaline 1 mg IV after the second shock, then every second cycle.
    • Give amiodarone 300 mg IV after the third shock; a further 150 mg may be considered.
  • Non-shockable rhythm: give adrenaline 1 mg IV as soon as access is available, then every second cycle. Give no shocks.
  • Airway: an advanced airway (supraglottic airway or endotracheal tube) is placed by a skilled operator without interrupting compressions. After that, compressions are continuous, with about 10 breaths a minute. Waveform capnography confirms tube placement and helps monitor CPR quality.
  • IV or IO access: use either for drugs.

Reversible causes: the 4 Hs and 4 Ts in Collin

  • Hypoxia: unlikely; he was talking normally just before he collapsed.
  • Hypovolaemia: possible bleeding on dual antiplatelets and enoxaparin, but his haemoglobin is normal.
  • Hypothermia or hyperthermia: not a factor on a ward.
  • Hypokalaemia, hyperkalaemia and other metabolic causes: his potassium (3.2 to 3.3) and magnesium (0.62) are low, probably from indapamide, and both lower the threshold for VF. ANZCOR lists potassium chloride (5 mmol IV bolus) for persistent VF with documented or suspected hypokalaemia, and magnesium sulfate (5 mmol IV) for hypomagnesaemia or torsades. His glucose is not low, and the acidosis is an expected result of the arrest.
  • Tension pneumothorax: no trauma or central line; examine the chest if there is doubt.
  • Tamponade: free wall rupture after infarction is usually later and causes PEA.
  • Toxins: none apparent.
  • Thrombosis, coronary: the most likely cause, given his NSTEMI and rising troponin.
  • Thrombosis, pulmonary: less likely because he is on therapeutic enoxaparin.

The other results

  • Venous gas: the mixed respiratory and lactic acidosis reflects the low blood flow and inadequate ventilation of cardiac arrest. It is treated with high-quality CPR and ventilation, not routine bicarbonate.
  • Troponin: the rise from 46 to 2850 ng/L confirms an evolving infarct.

After ROSC (ANZCOR post-resuscitation therapy)

  • Reassess with ABCDE and record a 12-lead ECG.
  • Titrate oxygen to SpO2 92 to 98%, aim for normal CO2 and avoid hypotension.
  • Check and control glucose, and prevent fever.
  • Withhold metformin (lactic acidosis and planned contrast) and review perindopril/indapamide while K and Mg are low.
  • Admit to ICU.
  • Emergency coronary angiography is indicated after ROSC with ST elevation, and should be considered when a coronary cause is likely, as it is here. At a regional hospital this means an urgent discussion with interventional cardiology and retrieval to a PCI-capable centre.
  • A senior clinician should contact his wife early.
  • Document times, rhythms, shocks and drugs.

Looking after the team

Sam did the most important thing: he recognised the collapse and called for help straight away. A hot debrief after the resuscitation, and follow-up support for junior staff and students, are part of good practice after a Code Blue.
points: In an unresponsive patient, slow noisy gasps are not normal breathing, and a few seconds of jerking at collapse is usually hypoxic jerking, not a seizure. Start compressions straight away; do not wait for a pulse check.

DRSABCD: Danger, Response, Send for help, Airway (suction, then a Guedel sized from the angle of the mandible to the centre of the incisors), Breathing (no more than 10 seconds), CPR 30:2 at 100 to 120 a minute to one third of the chest depth, and Defibrillation as soon as possible.
VF shows chaotic, irregular deflections of varying amplitude with no P waves, QRS complexes or T waves. VF and pulseless VT are shockable; asystole and PEA are not.

Shockable arm: single shocks with 2 minutes of CPR immediately after each, adrenaline 1 mg after the second shock and then every second cycle, and amiodarone 300 mg after the third shock. Non-shockable arm: adrenaline 1 mg as soon as access is available, then every second cycle.
Work through the 4 Hs and 4 Ts using the patient's own history and results. Here the cause is coronary thrombosis, with low potassium and magnesium (from indapamide) contributing.

Once the team takes over, get the history that changes management: the events before the collapse, the reason for admission, resuscitation status, medicines and recent results. After ROSC, plan ICU care and urgent angiography, and debrief the team.
